questions.q: Why does the well-architected guidance treat partition key choice as unusually high-stakes compared to most other Cosmos DB settings?
options: It's effectively immutable — changing it later requires creating a new container and migrating all the data
It has no real impact on performance or cost
It can be changed instantly with a single portal setting at any time
It only affects storage cost, never query performance
questions.explain: Unlike RU/s or consistency level, which can be adjusted on a live container, the partition key can't be changed without a full migration to a new container.

questions.q: What are the three qualities the lesson's partition key checklist looks for?
options: High cardinality, even access distribution, and a match to the dominant query pattern
Low cardinality, uneven distribution, and random query patterns
Alphabetical ordering, short string length, and no duplicates
Matching the primary key of the original relational table exactly
questions.explain: These three qualities together let throughput spread across physical partitions, avoid hot partitions, and keep most reads within a single partition.

questions.q: Per the well-architected cost guidance, what should be checked before simply raising provisioned RU/s to fix throttling?
options: Whether RU/s is really the constraint, rather than an inefficient query or a hot partition that more RU/s won't fix
Nothing — always raise RU/s first as the safest option
Whether the Azure subscription has enough credit remaining
Whether the container's name follows naming conventions
questions.explain: RU/s is billed whether used or not, so the guidance treats raising it as a last resort after confirming it's actually the bottleneck.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does Cosmos DB's default Session consistency level guarantee?
options: A single client always reads its own writes
All clients everywhere always see the absolute latest write instantly
No guarantee at all — reads can return arbitrarily stale or out-of-order data
Writes are only visible after a 24-hour delay
questions.explain: Session consistency guarantees read-your-own-writes for a given client, covering most real application needs at lower latency and RU cost than Strong.

questions.q: When does the lesson say it makes sense to move away from the default Session consistency level toward Eventual?
options: For read-heavy, latency-sensitive scenarios where brief staleness is genuinely acceptable, like a product catalog
For a financial balance check that can never tolerate staleness
Never — Eventual consistency should not be used under any circumstances
Only when migrating away from SQL Server entirely
questions.explain: Eventual trades staleness tolerance for the lowest possible read latency and RU cost, which fits read-heavy, latency-sensitive workloads like a catalog or leaderboard.
